cards.back: An antigen is a **molecule** recognised by a specific lymphocyte receptor or antibody. It is found on pathogens, toxins and cells from other individuals.

cards.front: Why does an antibody bind only one type of antigen?
cards.back: The **variable region** has a specific amino acid sequence, which gives its binding site a three-dimensional shape complementary to just one antigen.
cards.hint: Compare how a key fits a lock.

cards.front: What are the three main ways antibodies help destroy pathogens?
cards.back: **Agglutination**, marking and **neutralisation**. Antibodies mark and disable pathogens, but other cells do the engulfing.

cards.front: Which region of an antibody forms the antigen-binding site?
cards.back: The **variable region**, at the tips of the two arms. The rest of the molecule, the **constant region**, is similar in all antibodies.
cards.hint: Look at where the arms meet the rest of the Y.

cards.front: What is the structure of an antibody?
cards.back: A **Y-shaped** protein made of four polypeptide chains: two long heavy chains and two shorter light chains, held together by disulfide bonds.

cards.front: Which cells secrete antibodies into blood and tissue fluid?
cards.back: **Plasma cells**, which are specialised white blood cells.

cards.front: How does agglutination help phagocytes destroy pathogens?
cards.back: Each antibody binds two pathogens, so they **clump together**. Clumps are easier for phagocytes to find and engulf.

cards.front: How does neutralisation stop a toxin from causing harm?
cards.back: Bound antibodies **block** the toxin or a pathogen's attachment molecules, so it can no longer harm or enter host cells.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to say antibodies engulf and digest pathogens?
cards.back: Antibodies are **proteins**, not cells. They mark and disable pathogens, and **phagocytes** do the engulfing.
cards.hint: Think about what type of molecule an antibody is.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to say a bacterium is a single antigen?
cards.back: An antigen is a **molecule**, not a whole pathogen. A single bacterium can carry many different antigens.

cards.front: Why can a pathogen that changes its surface antigen escape existing antibodies?
cards.back: The new antigen has a different shape, so the **variable region** of the existing antibodies is no longer complementary and cannot bind it.
cards.hint: Think about what decides an antibody's binding-site shape.

cards.front: What happens when a pathogen changes its surface antigen?
cards.back: The immune system must make **new antibodies** with a matching variable region. This takes time, so the pathogen can multiply meanwhile.
cards.hint: Consider what happens to existing antibodies first.

cards.front: Why can antibodies not destroy a virus inside a host cell?
cards.back: Antibodies stay in blood and tissue fluid and act on pathogens **outside cells**, so they cannot reach a virus until the cell releases it.
cards.hint: Where in the body do antibodies stay?

cards.back: A **white blood cell** that has receptors able to recognise one specific antigen.
